title: Design a shared document editor
dek: A restaurant's owner, chef and manager edit their Zotato menu together: one adds a dish while another changes a price, each seeing the other's changes as they type. Build editing where nobody's change is lost, and everyone ends up with the same menu.

items: Don't save whole documents: the last save would wipe out the other person's change. Send small edits instead (insert this, delete that).
Give each document one server that owns it at a time. It puts every edit in one order, numbers it, saves it to the document's log, and sends it to everyone else.
Edits made at the same moment were made against an older version. Adjust the later one for what landed first (operational transforms), so both survive.
Save a snapshot every few hundred edits, so opening a document is a snapshot plus a few recent edits, not its whole history.
Cursors and "who's here" are sent but never saved; losing one costs nothing.
Several people edit the same document (a menu, a notice) at once and see each other's changes within half a second.
No change is ever lost, and everyone ends up with exactly the same text.
Show who else is in the document and where they're typing.
Out of scope here: rich formatting and images (the same ideas apply), and comments.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Your own typing appears instantly; others' within half a second
Every edit that was acknowledged is in the document
All editors end with identical text
20,000 documents open at the morning peak, 40,000 people editing

items: Documents: 3 lakh restaurants, a menu of about 20 KB each. All of them fit in 6 GB; size isn't the problem.
Open at once: about 20,000 documents with 40,000 editors at the morning peak, when kitchens update the day's menus.
Edits: phones send typing in small batches every 200 ms or so. At about 1 batch a second per active editor, that's around 40,000 edits a second at peak.
Servers: if one server comfortably holds 2,000 open documents with their editors' connections, that's 10 servers, more with room to spare.
The log: about 100 bytes an edit, 40,000 a second during peak hours, is about 4 MB a second, roughly 15 GB per peak hour. Snapshots let old edits be archived.
Document: `id`, `owner_restaurant`, `latest_seq`, `snapshot_seq`, `snapshot` (text at that number).
Edit: `doc_id`, `seq` (the server's order), `author`, `client_edit_id`, `base_seq` (the version the author saw), `ops` (insert or delete at a position).
Access: who may view or edit each document.

body.label: Over the open connection
body.say: Open a document and get its text and number. Send an edit with the version you made it on; get back its number. Receive others' edits in order. Share your cursor.

body.cap: Everyone editing menu #214 talks to the one doc server that owns it. The server orders each edit, numbers it into the document's log and sends it to the others; every few hundred edits it saves a snapshot.

body.x: One owner per document makes ordering simple: there's exactly one place deciding which edit came first. A registry (kept with consensus, as in the consensus article) says which server owns which document, and moves ownership if a server dies.

body.name: First try
body.what: Each editor sends the whole menu when they stop typing; the server keeps the latest.
body.use: Simple, fine when one person edits at a time.
body.avoid: Ananya saves her new dish; a second later Rohit saves his price change, made on the old menu. Ananya's dish is gone, and nobody notices until a customer asks.
body.ex: The chef adds "Paneer Tikka"; the manager's price update, saved after, quietly removes it.
body.like: Two people editing copies of the same printout and the last one to hand it in wins.

body.name: Better
body.what: Send each change as a small edit with the version it was made on. The doc server puts edits in one order; if an edit was made on an older version, it adjusts the edit's positions for the edits that came first, then applies and sends it.
body.use: Both changes survive, everyone applies the same edits in the same order, and everyone ends with the same text.
body.avoid: The adjusting rules (operational transforms) are fiddly to get right for every pair of edit types; use a tested library rather than writing your own.
body.ex: Rohit's price change made on #40 is shifted by the 7 characters Ananya added in #41, and both appear.
body.like: A secretary who takes changes from everyone and fixes the line numbers in each before typing it in.

body.cap: "Tikka ₹220": Ananya adds "Paneer " while Rohit changes 220 to 240. The server takes Ananya's first, shifts Rohit's change right by her 7 characters, and everyone ends with "Paneer Tikka ₹240".

body.x: The other approach is data types that merge on their own (CRDTs): every character gets a unique id, so edits can be applied in any order and still agree. They suit offline-first apps and peer-to-peer syncing; they cost more memory. With a server always in the middle, ordered and adjusted edits are simpler.

items: Show your edit on your screen at once, and keep it in a "sent, not yet confirmed" list.
When others' edits arrive, adjust each incoming edit past your unconfirmed ones before showing it, and your unconfirmed edits past it, so your screen matches what the server will have.
When the server confirms your edit with its number, drop it from the list.
The edit is saved to the log before it's confirmed; a server crash loses no confirmed edit.
Every few hundred edits, save a snapshot. Opening a document is the latest snapshot plus the edits after it.

An editor whose connection drops reconnects with its last number and gets everything after it, then resends its unconfirmed edits with their ids and the version each was made on. The server adjusts each one for the edits it missed; if it already has that id, it just sends back the number it gave it.
A doc server dies: the registry gives its documents to other servers, which load the snapshot and log. Editors reconnect and resend unconfirmed edits.
Someone edits offline for an hour: their edits are adjusted against an hour of others' edits when they reconnect. For long offline work, CRDTs or a "review changes" step work better.

Two servers think they own a document (a pause during a handover): the log only accepts writes carrying the current owner's token, a number the registry raises at every handover (fencing), so one of them is refused.
Junior / mid: open connections, sending edits not whole documents, a server that orders them.
Senior: one owner per document, adjusting concurrent edits, local edits shown at once, snapshots plus a log.
Lead: the registry and moving ownership, fencing during handover, OT versus CRDTs and when each fits, reconnecting and offline edits.
"See the menu as it was last Tuesday?" Replay the log from the snapshot before Tuesday up to the last edit of Tuesday.
"Undo?" Undo your own last edit by sending its opposite as a new edit, adjusted like any other; never rewind the shared log.
"A document with 500 editors?" Rare for menus; batch edits more and send cursors less often, or split very large documents.
"Permissions change mid-edit?" The server checks access on every edit, not only when opening.
"How do you test it?" Simulate many editors making random edits at once, in random orders and with dropped connections, and check every copy ends identical.

body.x: Doc servers hold open connections, like chat gateways. The first lesson is the same as any server's: one isn't enough.

practice.brief: Each test sends edit batches. Each one is appended to its document's log: 1 query. An edit is acknowledged once it is in the log; applying it to snapshots can follow. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

checks.label: Everyone in a document gets others' edits over connections that stay open
Edits are merged in order by a part that takes them from a queue
Edits are stored in order so the document can be replayed

tests.name: The morning peak
tests.desc: 40,000 edit batches a second at 10 am, when kitchens update the day's menus.

tests.name: Menu change day
tests.desc: At 8 pm every restaurant changes prices for a festival: 80,000 edit batches a second for 15 minutes.

checks.label: Edits go through an ordered log (queue)

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (40,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of edits still succeed
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of edits still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (10,000 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

tests.name: Type in a document
tests.desc: u1's edit becomes version 42 of document d1.

est.label: Edit batches a second at peak

decisions.q: Two people type in the same paragraph at once. What happens?
options: The paragraph is locked for whoever started typing first
OT or CRDTs merge both edits the same way on every copy
Each save replaces the paragraph; the last save wins
decisions.why: Locks get in the way of writing together, and "last save wins" loses work. Operational transforms or CRDTs make every copy end up the same with both edits kept.

options: The whole document saved again after every change made
The document saved only when someone presses Save
Every edit added to a log, with a snapshot now and then
decisions.why: Small edits are cheap to add and keep history; snapshots mean nobody replays a year of edits to open the document. Saving the whole document per keystroke is heavy, and waiting for Save loses unsaved work.

decisions.q: How do other people's cursors and edits appear?
options: Pushed over open connections to everyone in the document
Each app asks the server for any new changes every 10 seconds
Each app asks for changes whenever its user types
decisions.why: Writing together only feels live if edits arrive within a fraction of a second, even while you aren't typing. Polling is either slow or wasteful.

hints.x: Three properties fight each other: instant typing, no lost edits, identical results. Name all three.
Editors × batches a second gives edits a second; open documents ÷ documents per server gives servers.
Open a document (snapshot and its sequence number), send edits based on the sequence you saw, receive others' edits with theirs.
Each document's edits get one order in a log. In the Lab, a Queue between the edit servers and the workers that persist.
40,000 edits a second is more than one database: several share the documents.
Two groups of edit servers and workers, Multi-AZ databases: an acknowledged edit survives a crash.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: No queue
wrong.why: The burst hits the database directly and crashes it.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.

wrong.name: Edits keyed by a random id
wrong.why: Each edit is keyed by an id the client doesn't send, and nothing keeps edits of a document in order.
